title: Mid-term warm-up: C basics (HackerRank style)
overview: These five short C programs are HackerRank-style exam problems on the fundamentals: nested loops, if/else ranges, counting, running sums and string comparison. They are quick to write but easy to get slightly wrong, so they are good for checking that input reading, boundaries and output format are all right.

concepts.term: Read into an array, then process
concepts.explain: Read all `N` values with `scanf` into an array first, then loop again to compute the answer. Keeping reading and logic apart makes each loop simple.
"Between X and Y" usually includes both ends, so the test is `p >= X && p <= Y`. Off-by-one mistakes at the edges are the most common wrong answer.
When items are sorted from smallest to largest, taking them in order and stopping when the total goes over the limit gives the maximum count.
`strcmp(a, b)` returns a negative number if `a` comes first in dictionary order, 0 if equal, positive if later. Copy strings with `strcpy`, never with `=`.
A sum of up to 10^5 values can pass the `int` limit (about 2.1 × 10^9). Use `long long` with `%lld`.

files.title: Do it: print 1..K, N times
files.what: Prints the numbers `1` to `K` on one line, and repeats that line `N` times, using two nested loops.
steps: Outer loop runs `N` times — one per line.
Inner loop prints `j` from `1` to `K`, each followed by a space.
After the inner loop, print `\n` to finish the line.
files.output_note: Three lines, each `1 2 3 4 ` (with a trailing space, which the judge accepts).
files.watch_out: Print the newline in the outer loop, not the inner one; otherwise every number ends up on its own line.

check.q: How many numbers are printed in total for `N = 7`, `K = 4`?

files.title: Job application: classify by experience
files.what: Reads `N` experience values and prints a category for each using an if / else-if chain over ranges.
files.input_note: `N`, then `N` experience values (spaces or newlines both work with `scanf`).
files.output_note: One line per candidate in input order: Mid-level, Entry-level, Junior, Senior, Junior.
files.watch_out: Because the chain is `else if`, the `>= 1` and `>= 4` parts are already guaranteed — they are harmless but not needed. `int experiences[100000]` on the stack is about 400 KB; fine here, but large arrays are safer as globals.

check.q: Which category does experience `7` fall into?

files.title: Price range: count values in [X, Y]
files.what: Counts how many phone prices fall inside the inclusive range `X..Y`.
steps: For each price, add 1 to `count` if `prices[i] >= X && prices[i] <= Y`.
files.input_note: `N X Y`, then `N` prices. This is the problem's own sample (expected `4`).
files.output_note: `4` — the prices 8, 7, 8 and 5 are inside 4..8. Both 8s count because the range is inclusive.
files.watch_out: `long long prices[100000]` is about 800 KB of stack memory; move it outside `main` if you ever see a crash on big input.

check.q: If the range were exclusive, what would the answer be for the sample?
check.a: `2` — only 7 and 5 are strictly between 4 and 8.

files.title: Book reading: how many books fit in T
files.what: The reading times are sorted, so reading the shortest books first gives the most books. The code keeps a running total and stops once it exceeds `T`.
steps: If the total is still `<= T`, count the book.
Otherwise `break` — no later (longer) book can fit either.
files.input_note: `N T`, then `N` times in increasing order. This is the problem's sample (expected `6`).
files.output_note: `6` — 1+3+4+6+8+10 = 32 fits in 33; adding 12 makes 44, which is too much.
files.watch_out: `total_time` must be `long long`: 10^5 books of large times can overflow `int`.

check.q: Why is it safe to `break` at the first book that doesn't fit?
check.a: The list is increasing, so every later book is at least as long and cannot fit either.

files.title: Lexicographic min and max of 3 strings
files.what: Finds the dictionary-smallest and dictionary-largest of three words using `strcmp` and `strcpy`.
steps: Start both `min` and `max` as copies of `S1`.
If `strcmp(S2, min) < 0` or `strcmp(S3, min) < 0`, copy that string into `min`.
files.complexity: Time O(L) where L is the string length · Space O(L)
files.input_note: Three lowercase words on one line.
files.watch_out: Arrays are size `1001` so a 1000-letter word plus the `\0` fits. `min = S2` would not compile for arrays — use `strcpy`.

check.q: What is the lexicographic minimum of `ab`, `abc`, `b`?
check.a: `ab` — a prefix comes before the longer word.

recap: Nested loops: outer = rows, inner = items in a row.
Check range edges carefully: inclusive means `>=` and `<=`.
Sorted input + running sum + `break` = greedy maximum count.
`strcmp` for order, `strcpy` for copying C strings.
Use `long long` for sums that can pass 2 × 10^9.

check_yourself.q: What does `strcmp("cat", "car")` return: negative, zero or positive?
In the book problem, what goes wrong if the times were not sorted?
check_yourself.a: Taking books in the given order may stop early on a long book while shorter ones later could still fit, so the count would not be the maximum.

check_yourself.q: In `price_range.c`, what is printed if the input gives `X > Y` (for example `X = 8`, `Y = 4`)?
check_yourself.a: `0` — no price can be both `>= 8` and `<= 4`.

body: This page is a short step back into C. After vectors, classes and linked lists it can feel odd to write `scanf` again, but that is the point of a warm-up: the exam that follows is on the fundamentals, and the fundamentals are where careless marks are lost.

Nothing here is new. The five programs use only a loop, an `if`, an array, and two functions from `<string.h>`. What they test is whether you still get the small things right: reading the input in the right order, treating the edges of a range correctly, and choosing a type that is big enough.
Four of the five programs have exactly the same shape. Read everything first, then work on it:
intro.trace:
read N
loop N times   -> store each value in an array
loop N times   -> decide / count / add up
print the one answer

body: You could do both jobs in one loop, and for these problems that would work. Two loops are still worth the extra lines, because each loop then does one thing and you can read it and see that it is right. That is the habit an exam rewards.
**The worked example.** `price_range.c` asks how many phone prices fall between `X` and `Y`. Take the sample: `X = 4`, `Y = 8`, and ten prices.

"Between 4 and 8" includes 4 and 8 themselves, so the test needs `>=` and `<=`. Write `>` by mistake and the two eights stop counting and the answer becomes 2. This single character is the most common wrong answer on problems of this kind, so read the statement twice before you write the condition.
The whole program is then four lines of logic:

**A second shape.** `book_reading.c` gives reading times already sorted from short to long and a total time `T`. You add times one by one and stop the moment the total passes `T`. With `T = 33` and the times `1 3 4 6 8 10 12 15 23 36` the running total goes 1, 4, 8, 14, 22, 32, then 44 — too much — so the answer is 6 books. Because the list is sorted, taking the short books first can never be beaten, and a single `break` ends the loop.

**A third shape.** `lexic_min_max.c` works on strings instead of numbers. The idea is the old min/max one: keep the answer in a variable and replace it when something better arrives. Only the two operations change — `strcmp(a, b)` for "which comes first in dictionary order", `strcpy(dst, src)` for copying, because `=` does not copy a C string.

**What to watch for.** Sums of up to 100000 values can pass the `int` limit of about 2.1 billion, so keep totals in `long long` and print them with `%lld`. Check the edges of every range. Match the output format exactly, including the newline after each line in `do_it.c`.
The five programs below each show the full statement, the code and a trace of the sample input.
